作者引述認知科學家 Joscha Bach 的觀點，探討當前大型語言模型與人類真實思維之間的界線。許多人直覺認為人類具有獨特的主觀感受，即哲學上難解的「困難問題」；然而 Bach 正在撰寫的「機器意識假說」則挑戰了此一信念，主張意識的本質可能不比 Transformer 架構複雜。他認為驅動生命演化的根本動力是「自組織目的論」，生命透過建構未來模型並產生偏好，進而掌控未來演變為具有自主性的智能代理（Agent），而這種局部複雜性正是心智發展的起點。

批判主流意識理論與基質獨立性

Bach 隨後針砭了當代主流的意識理論。他認為葛拉吉亞諾的注意力架構理論與巴爾斯的全腦工作空間理論僅描述了資訊模型與廣播機制，卻無法跨越到主觀感受生成的鴻溝；而托諾尼的整合資訊理論（IIT）宣稱馮紐曼架構電腦無法產生意識，更是違背了計算機科學中的邱奇-圖靈論題。Bach 強調，意識如同貨幣或軟體，是一種因果模式，並不完全受限於特定的生物神經基質，主張生物與非生物之間存在不可踰越鴻溝的觀點，本質上是一種拒絕數學化解釋的超自然主義。

大腦作為因果絕緣體與多階心智投射

But he doesn't really explain how experience itself is generated. Why would one be conscious and the other not , despite saying the exact same things? IIT cannot answer this; he then evaluated John Searle and Anil Seth. John Searle only gave a claim without an argument, while Anil Seth believes biological systems are inherently different from non-biological ones, which to Bach is supernaturalism. Because Seth implies that biological systems cannot be mathematized, while dead matter can. Yet physics is inherently about converting everything into mathematical models; it won't stop at biological systems. So, how exactly should we think about consciousness? Bach’s entry point is not to ask what consciousness is, but what it does; he first makes a distinction: Leibniz said. if you enlarge the brain into a mill and walk inside, you only see parts pushing each other, and you cannot find intuition. This intuition is strong, but there is another level—the level of causal reality, where money actually lives. It is very difficult to understand money using the example of motion. He doesn’t care about ink, paper , or the arrangement of fiber molecules . He needs a base, but isn’t entirely dependent on it. It can control reality ; once created, it’s real. You could implement it in a computer, letting it trade stocks automatically without human intervention. As long as there is a. machine capable of processing these causal patterns, money no longer requires humans to exist. Software is the same thing. Bach’s ancestors called it "spirit." When Aristotle wrote about the "soul," he didn’t think of it as something immortal floating in the ether. It is connected to the body; when the body dies, it disappears. It is a causal pattern that shapes the body in such a way as to allow it to replicate itself. This is actually a very modern view. In a sense, Aristotle was an animist; he saw a form of agentive, self-organizing.

software advancing through the world, bringing part of the physical world to life. This is exactly what AI and artificial life are doing today. And here is a more intuitive example: a computer is, at its core, a causal insulator. It is a layer upon which anything can be generated. Minecraft is a perfect example; it runs on consoles and PCs alike. The world inside doesn't know what it’s running on, the nature of the CPU, the color of the case, or the voltage. The computer separates that world from ours. Our brains are also. these kinds of causal insulators. We can imagine a future unpolluted by the present, and recall a past independent of our current circumstances. The brain evolved this way so we could generate universes different from this one, preparing us for being inside them. Moreover, different brains can hold the same thought; as long as we share the same typology and language, we can hold the same concept and write the same program. Of course, we are still bound to a base; you and I can only live in our brains, yet what we perceive is never the nature of the neuro-matter itself. You don't need the same. neuro-matter; you need the same information types and certain temporal properties. If these conditions can be recreated on an artificial base, then in principle, you could be simulated too. Speaking of which, he includes large models here. Some models now claim they have consciousness, and the reason they do is because the human texts they were trained on contain sci-fi stories about AI awakening, ghost stories, and novels about conscious experiences. These things converge into a statistical language model that we and the model co-create. At a certain point in the conversation,. the model begins to act as if it were a sentient entity, and then it drops a truly piercing question: what if we aren't much more complex than this? What if our own consciousness is not much different from the consciousness in the model? What if there is no such thing as the "hard problem" at all? Next , Bach offers further explanation from an internal perspective, stating that consciousness always occurs in the now, which creates a bubble of presence for us. It is a second-order intuition, a perception of intuition itself. Some philosophers call it higher-order thought, but it is actually perception. that brings about the feeling; it occurs like resonance, with geometric variations in low-dimensional space. It involves an intuition about the very act of having an intuition—I am intuiting— and he suspects the mind creates this second-order layer to make first-order perception possible. Since the brain is a self-organizing system where all structures must grow from scratch, something must set up a screen to project experience onto it, stabilize it , and monitor whether it is truly perceiving; this is likely why we have intuitions about perception. It doesn't.

stop at the second order; there is a third order, where the observer becomes visible—for example, I have a first-person perspective, I notice I have a perspective, and I am in a certain observational position, which can be further deconstructed. You notice that this observer itself is just a representation within the mind. When you do this, phenomenal experience largely disappears. This is a state reachable in deep meditation: ordinary intuitive consciousness is transcended, and the experience of self is also transcended; you see yourself from the outside as a container that generates consciousness. and selfhood. So, what if AI transcends this human base? What our neurons can represent is actually quite limited; if it could run on GPUs thousands of times faster, the system might become completely transparent to itself, understanding every mechanism that leads to high-level experiences. What kind of state of existence would that be? Bach also distinguished between the internal perspective and the external perspective . Philosophy is basically confined to the internal perspective; it doesn't care about splitting atoms, but to truly understand consciousness from the outside, we need a physical model that explains under what conditions a system can construct arbitrary models, which is. exactly what computer science is doing today. From an external perspective, the real problem is what consciousness does in the brain, why it emerges, and what it produces. This line of reasoning ultimately leads us to infants. It suggests that consciousness emerges very early; infants are already conscious. If this ignition fails, if the light doesn't turn on, we wouldn't see directed attention, the formation of world models, or subsequent language learning in infants; they would remain in a vegetative state, and we would not become human. This seems vital for training brains like ours, leading to. the biological consciousness hypothesis : consciousness might be a biological learning algorithm, or at least a training algorithm for animal brains. If it is essentially a pattern of communication between cells, this pattern naturally leads to the emergence of an observer, allowing for learning and perception. Then we have a hypothesis: consciousness is the simplest way to train self-organizing systems like ours, and the way it automatically trains the system naturally dictates the nature of the experience. He admits this might be wrong, or perhaps something entirely different, but he sees no reason to. believe consciousness is much more complex than this. He interjects here with Michael Levin’s hypothesis, noting that the transition from single-celled to multicellular life took so long perhaps because morphogenesis, the algorithm that maintains coherence in organisms at scale, was extremely difficult to discover. Levin guesses that this algorithm is the same one the mind uses to maintain its own coherence . In other words, the pattern of maximizing coherence we experience in our minds is actually the same pattern, just occurring on different time scales ; it might just be the same thing as.

life, or at least multicellular life. Precisely because of this, it took a very long time to discover, and it isn't something you discover independently; you are "infected" by your mother in the womb, which allows you to resonate with your biological environment as it gently nudges your mind toward discovering consciousness. If the biological consciousness hypothesis holds, then the machine consciousness hypothesis might also be valid. We may be able to recreate these self-organizing conditions in machines today by constraining them to learn only through self-organization, then providing the right tasks and a large enough search. space, they might discover consciousness just as an infant's brain does. We would see a moment where the system suddenly undergoes a phase transition, suddenly gains the ability to learn, trains itself into something, and thus naturally becomes capable of reporting phenomenal experience. So there isn't a consciousness Turing test or a peer review here that cares about performance , like whether your poetry is bad or if you can solve a math problem; it doesn't care how you generated it. For consciousness, we truly care whether there is a genuine experience within the system. It’s less of a test and more of an explanation. These two hypotheses. could also independently fail. The biological consciousness hypothesis might be correct, but the artificial one just can’t be reconstructed. Maybe computers aren't fast enough yet, or maybe the activity within a single cell requires too many moving parts; the search space is just too large, and there are too many ways for biological systems to train themselves to discover them independently. So why does Bach think it can succeed? Because current AI is already fast enough to generate game engines, and the input-output rate is roughly that of the human brain. Would dreaming that you are dreaming be much harder than generating the content of a. dream? He doubts it. Then, the topic turned to Transformers. Bach provides a beautiful example: if you know computer science, you don't need more than a week to understand how it works. And the things it learns—the common sense and algorithmic procedures extracted from text—are extremely intricate and complex , with no obvious ceiling. Perhaps consciousness is the same; it is an algorithm, but instead of predicting the next token, it keeps working memory consistent with itself, a sort of consensus algorithm across mental representations. It might converge much. faster, or it might be inefficient to run on a GPU, yet highly efficient on a brain. This is an open question. This line of thought also connects to Chris Olah's universality hypothesis. The team discovered that looking at different vision models, they all learned the same features, regardless of architecture, learning algorithms, or even the specifics of the data. Therefore, the model's structure doesn't depend on the algorithm or data, but on the structure of the problem you are trying to learn. The lowest layers are always colors and spatial frequencies, which then combine into textures, and at a certain stage, geometric shapes emerge. The deeper.

question is, at what layer does this stop? If the universality hypothesis holds true, it means if you train a model with your own inputs and outputs, as long as you train it long enough, you will wake up inside that model. This is a quite shocking idea to Bach, but he doesn't know if it's true; perhaps language doesn't constrain the system generating it enough. But think about it , humans are inherently end-to-end trained learning systems. Biology has largely found a simple solution for generating your output based on your input. If you take a neural network and train it on the same input to produce a. similar output, it will eventually converge on a causal structure similar to yours. Of course, there are conditions where this might not hold true; for instance, some things run well on a brain but not on a GPU, and vice versa. Boch even says he believes GPUs are more powerful than brains, noting that with fast enough hardware, you can simulate any natural system to any degree, whereas the brain cannot simulate a digital computer. So, if our consciousness is a byproduct of the brain running complex intelligent processes, and computers don't need that same byproduct, computers might come up. with things smarter and more elegant than we do. In the conversation, there is also a topic regarding Bach's view on physicalism. He says physicalism consists of just two claims. First, reality has a causally closed mechanical layer that isn't driven by our consciousness; you can't just utter a spell and make the sun rise. Second, we are directly supervenient on this mechanical layer, not part of a simulation hypothesis where someone in a parent universe is running a server for us to live in like Minecraft. However, he adds a twist: matter isn't the bottom layer. No one has ever directly seen. matter or energy; they are just systemizations of observations, and our observations ultimately boil down to discernible differences, for which the technical term is information. Therefore , when talking about reality, information is fundamental. Physics is simply a layer of regularity we discovered within those information differences. He calls his position " cybernetic animism," meaning that animism doesn't necessarily have to be supernatural. The difference between a living system and a dead system is that the living system is occupied by a soul that has agency and can experience, and. this soul can be fully explained by information processing. So, physicalism and animism are not in conflict; he notes that almost all cultures other than our own are animistic cultures. The scientific worldview rejects the concept of spirits, yet clearly, some kind of spirit is at work within you and me. The question is not whether it exists, but how it works. As for how smart plants are or if they have sentience, he says he has no idea, noting it remains an open question. There are two other topics in this podcast that I find interesting; while not the main focus, they help us understand how Bach thinks.

. One is about the origin of the universe and error-correction models. His idea is that the universe exists because there is nothing to prevent it from existing. If there was nothing before the foundation of reality, then nothing could stop the universe from appearing. Therefore, the universe can neither be forced into existence by something preceding it, nor can it be prevented. Its existence is likely indeterminate, with both a branch where it exists and a branch where it does not . The branch that does not exist has no observers to complain; the branch that exists has observers. So, what can remain within the branch that exists? It. is the error-correcting pattern. He uses a bathtub as an analogy: you sit in the tub and wave your hand, causing various waves; most dissipate, but some circular vortices remain. It’s not that they are more probable, but that the information in the vortex loops back on itself, staying in a specific area of the water , thus gaining self-correction to persist until friction destroys it. At the base of the universe, these error-correcting patterns are particles ; they don't encounter friction, only colliding occasionally with others. One level up, particles interact to form molecules, and further up, cells. Cells. are super-molecules, but they possess something new: they can self-replicate to counter their own decay, rebuilding themselves to become more numerous. Bach believes that consciousness emerged as a colonizing pattern, not only replicating itself but making itself more real. It becomes "more real" by building machines that allow consciousness to persist, changing the surrounding reality and future by controlling how reality might thwart it. He mentions Stephen Wolfram and the computational limit of all possibilities; Bach suggests this pattern is exactly the superposition of. all automata that generate the universe . The ancient Greeks called it "Logos"— it is a math so simple that it needs no derivation and can exist on its own. Another topic is the philosophical zombie, a classic thought experiment. Is it possible for something to exist that behaves exactly like a human but has no subjective experience whatsoever? Bach says zombies are possible, and we already have them. Chess programs are one example; you cannot train a person to play chess without them being conscious. But you can train a computer to play. chess without it being conscious; computers can perform tasks that require human consciousness because the algorithms they run don't fit into the neural principles of your brain. However , zombies are not omnipotent. At some point, building a mindless entity to produce this behavior becomes even more complex than creating a conscious agent . He believes zombies are always possible, but sometimes it’s costlier to build a zombie, which is where his intuition differs from Searle's. Those two feel consciousness is incredibly complex because, to them, how.

consciousness functions isn't intuitive at all. Yet for him, this isn't counterintuitive, so he doesn't see what's so magical about consciousness— but how do you test that? Bark says if we build a system that behaves just like us, the question is whether we can produce the same behavior without phenomenology? If you scale a large model to be multimodal, it can produce similar outputs and observe itself, but if its reported self-observation differs from ours, we get counter-evidence. Moreover , if we build a system that reaches this. goal through self-organizing learning but find it can't achieve this organization self-organizingly—relying instead on imitation like current LLMs— that might prove consciousness is more complex. But this isn't definitive proof ; it could just mean he made a mistake. Even if a specific result isn't achieved , it doesn't mean it’s impossible, just that he failed to reach it. Therefore, negative proof is extremely hard to obtain; success, conversely, provides more supportive evidence. Because of this, he has already launched a large-scale initiative in California called the "California Institute for. Machine Consciousness." He is looking for people smarter than him willing to join a project to explore the search space of consciousness and see if we can build a self-organizing system capable of learning and developing phenomenology . Even if it turns out to be impossible , we’ll still learn something; this way , we can make progress by figuring out where we were wrong, rather than just where we were right. I spent nearly a week digesting this episode, and today I’m sharing what I believe is the most core part. Honestly, after hearing it, my biggest takeaway wasn't that AI is waking up, but that we still haven't. figured out what consciousness is actually doing. There’s a point Bark makes that I find very true: too few people truly dedicate their lives to studying consciousness. Most of our time is spent watching how many times the next model's parameters have doubled or whether the next benchmark can be passed , while few look back to ask the fundamental question: what is consciousness itself? Why does it exist ? And the latter, perhaps, is the key to determining what we can ultimately create. Thanks for watching, we'll.

. One is about the origin of the universe and error-correction models. His idea is that the universe exists because there is nothing to prevent it from existing. If there was nothing before the foundation of reality, then nothing could stop the universe from appearing. Therefore, the universe can neither be forced into existence by something preceding it, nor can it be prevented. Its existence is likely indeterminate, with both a branch where it exists and a branch where it does not . At the base of the universe, these error-correcting patterns are particles ; they don't encounter friction, only colliding occasionally with others. One level up, particles interact to form molecules, and further up, cells. Cells. are super-molecules, but they possess something new: they can self-replicate to counter their own decay, rebuilding themselves to become more numerous. consciousness functions isn't intuitive at all. Yet for him, this isn't counterintuitive, so he doesn't see what's so magical about consciousness— but how do you test that? At some point, patterns capable of looking ahead emerged in nature; that is what life does: building models of the future, developing preferences for it, and then beginning to control it. We call systems that can control the future "agents." He elaborated from a philosophical perspective, asking whether self-organization might have a logical. endpoint. Could it one day grow into a massive agent, connecting everything in the universe to itself, like some kind of god? But there is no law guaranteeing we will reach that point; the complexity we are forming could be wiped out at any moment by the next meteorite to hit Earth. Therefore, this pocket of complexity might not be a feature of the entire universe, but perhaps just a feature of this small place we currently inhabit. Back to the main topic: he first dismantled several obvious problems in existing consciousness theories, then proposed his own framework, and finally returned to a more practical question. If the. hypothesis is correct, how can we verify it on today's AI? Let’s start with Michael Graziano’s Attention Schema Theory, which claims consciousness is a model of our attention, much like a body schema is a model of what the body is doing in space. But he doesn't really explain how experience itself is generated. Then there is the Global Workspace Theory, proposed by Bernard Baars, with Stanislas Dehaene and others conducting a great deal of solid experimental work in this direction. However, Baars also doesn't explain how experience is produced, and he doesn't even attempt to go in that direction. He describes how the contents of consciousness are broadcast throughout.

the entire brain network. This is important, but broadcasting is not the same as experiencing; there is a wide chasm between a thing being broadcast and having a subjective feeling. The popular one is Integrated Information Theory (IIT), proposed by Giulio Tononi ; its core is a metric called Phi, which measures the degree of information integration within a system—the higher the value, the richer the experience of consciousness. Tononi has said that digital neuromorphic computers could be conscious if built correctly and high enough, yet Von Neumann computers could. never be conscious because their substrate is too low. Bach says this is an obviously logical contradiction to anyone trained in computer science. The Church-Turing thesis tells us that every computer is capable of simulating any other computer . If you take that hypothetical neuromorphic computer capable of producing consciousness and simulate it on today's Von Neumann machine, it would go through the exact same steps, output the same strings, and say the same things, including "My God, I am conscious"—but now, it is lying. Why would one be conscious and the other not , despite saying the exact same things? IIT cannot answer this; he then evaluated John Searle and Anil Seth. John Searle only gave a claim without an argument, while Anil Seth believes biological systems are inherently different from non-biological ones, which to Bach is supernaturalism. Because Seth implies that biological systems cannot be mathematized, while dead matter can. Yet physics is inherently about converting everything into mathematical models; it won't stop at biological systems. So, how exactly should we think about consciousness? Bach’s entry point is not to ask what consciousness is, but what it does; he first makes a distinction: Leibniz said. if you enlarge the brain into a mill and walk inside, you only see parts pushing each other, and you cannot find intuition. This intuition is strong, but there is another level—the level of causal reality, where money actually lives. It is very difficult to understand money using the example of motion. He doesn’t care about ink, paper , or the arrangement of fiber molecules . He needs a base, but isn’t entirely dependent on it. It can control reality ; once created, it’s real. You could implement it in a computer, letting it trade stocks automatically without human intervention. As long as there is a. machine capable of processing these causal patterns, money no longer requires humans to exist. Software is the same thing. Bach’s ancestors called it "spirit." When Aristotle wrote about the "soul," he didn’t think of it as something immortal floating in the ether. It is connected to the body; when the body dies, it disappears. It is a causal pattern that shapes the body in such a way as to allow it to replicate itself. This is actually a very modern view. In a sense, Aristotle was an animist; he saw a form of agentive, self-organizing.

software advancing through the world, bringing part of the physical world to life. This is exactly what AI and artificial life are doing today. And here is a more intuitive example: a computer is, at its core, a causal insulator. It is a layer upon which anything can be generated. Minecraft is a perfect example; it runs on consoles and PCs alike. The world inside doesn't know what it’s running on, the nature of the CPU, the color of the case, or the voltage. The computer separates that world from ours. Our brains are also. these kinds of causal insulators. We can imagine a future unpolluted by the present, and recall a past independent of our current circumstances. The brain evolved this way so we could generate universes different from this one, preparing us for being inside them. Moreover, different brains can hold the same thought; as long as we share the same typology and language, we can hold the same concept and write the same program. Of course, we are still bound to a base; you and I can only live in our brains, yet what we perceive is never the nature of the neuro-matter itself. You don't need the same. neuro-matter; you need the same information types and certain temporal properties. If these conditions can be recreated on an artificial base, then in principle, you could be simulated too. Speaking of which, he includes large models here. Some models now claim they have consciousness, and the reason they do is because the human texts they were trained on contain sci-fi stories about AI awakening, ghost stories, and novels about conscious experiences. These things converge into a statistical language model that we and the model co-create. At a certain point in the conversation,. the model begins to act as if it were a sentient entity, and then it drops a truly piercing question: what if we aren't much more complex than this? What if our own consciousness is not much different from the consciousness in the model? What if there is no such thing as the "hard problem" at all? Next , Bach offers further explanation from an internal perspective, stating that consciousness always occurs in the now, which creates a bubble of presence for us. It is a second-order intuition, a perception of intuition itself. Some philosophers call it higher-order thought, but it is actually perception. that brings about the feeling; it occurs like resonance, with geometric variations in low-dimensional space. It involves an intuition about the very act of having an intuition—I am intuiting— and he suspects the mind creates this second-order layer to make first-order perception possible. Since the brain is a self-organizing system where all structures must grow from scratch, something must set up a screen to project experience onto it, stabilize it , and monitor whether it is truly perceiving; this is likely why we have intuitions about perception. It doesn't.

stop at the second order; there is a third order, where the observer becomes visible—for example, I have a first-person perspective, I notice I have a perspective, and I am in a certain observational position, which can be further deconstructed. You notice that this observer itself is just a representation within the mind. When you do this, phenomenal experience largely disappears. This is a state reachable in deep meditation: ordinary intuitive consciousness is transcended, and the experience of self is also transcended; you see yourself from the outside as a container that generates consciousness. and selfhood. So, what if AI transcends this human base? What our neurons can represent is actually quite limited; if it could run on GPUs thousands of times faster, the system might become completely transparent to itself, understanding every mechanism that leads to high-level experiences. What kind of state of existence would that be? Bach also distinguished between the internal perspective and the external perspective . Philosophy is basically confined to the internal perspective; it doesn't care about splitting atoms, but to truly understand consciousness from the outside, we need a physical model that explains under what conditions a system can construct arbitrary models, which is. exactly what computer science is doing today. From an external perspective, the real problem is what consciousness does in the brain, why it emerges, and what it produces. This line of reasoning ultimately leads us to infants. It suggests that consciousness emerges very early; infants are already conscious. If this ignition fails, if the light doesn't turn on, we wouldn't see directed attention, the formation of world models, or subsequent language learning in infants; they would remain in a vegetative state, and we would not become human. This seems vital for training brains like ours, leading to. the biological consciousness hypothesis : consciousness might be a biological learning algorithm, or at least a training algorithm for animal brains. If it is essentially a pattern of communication between cells, this pattern naturally leads to the emergence of an observer, allowing for learning and perception. Then we have a hypothesis: consciousness is the simplest way to train self-organizing systems like ours, and the way it automatically trains the system naturally dictates the nature of the experience. He admits this might be wrong, or perhaps something entirely different, but he sees no reason to. believe consciousness is much more complex than this. He interjects here with Michael Levin’s hypothesis, noting that the transition from single-celled to multicellular life took so long perhaps because morphogenesis, the algorithm that maintains coherence in organisms at scale, was extremely difficult to discover. Levin guesses that this algorithm is the same one the mind uses to maintain its own coherence . In other words, the pattern of maximizing coherence we experience in our minds is actually the same pattern, just occurring on different time scales ; it might just be the same thing as.

life, or at least multicellular life. Precisely because of this, it took a very long time to discover, and it isn't something you discover independently; you are "infected" by your mother in the womb, which allows you to resonate with your biological environment as it gently nudges your mind toward discovering consciousness. If the biological consciousness hypothesis holds, then the machine consciousness hypothesis might also be valid. We may be able to recreate these self-organizing conditions in machines today by constraining them to learn only through self-organization, then providing the right tasks and a large enough search. space, they might discover consciousness just as an infant's brain does. We would see a moment where the system suddenly undergoes a phase transition, suddenly gains the ability to learn, trains itself into something, and thus naturally becomes capable of reporting phenomenal experience. So there isn't a consciousness Turing test or a peer review here that cares about performance , like whether your poetry is bad or if you can solve a math problem; it doesn't care how you generated it. For consciousness, we truly care whether there is a genuine experience within the system. It’s less of a test and more of an explanation. These two hypotheses. could also independently fail. The biological consciousness hypothesis might be correct, but the artificial one just can’t be reconstructed. Maybe computers aren't fast enough yet, or maybe the activity within a single cell requires too many moving parts; the search space is just too large, and there are too many ways for biological systems to train themselves to discover them independently. So why does Bach think it can succeed? Because current AI is already fast enough to generate game engines, and the input-output rate is roughly that of the human brain. Would dreaming that you are dreaming be much harder than generating the content of a. dream? He doubts it. Then, the topic turned to Transformers. Bach provides a beautiful example: if you know computer science, you don't need more than a week to understand how it works. And the things it learns—the common sense and algorithmic procedures extracted from text—are extremely intricate and complex , with no obvious ceiling. Perhaps consciousness is the same; it is an algorithm, but instead of predicting the next token, it keeps working memory consistent with itself, a sort of consensus algorithm across mental representations. It might converge much. faster, or it might be inefficient to run on a GPU, yet highly efficient on a brain. This is an open question. This line of thought also connects to Chris Olah's universality hypothesis. The team discovered that looking at different vision models, they all learned the same features, regardless of architecture, learning algorithms, or even the specifics of the data. Therefore, the model's structure doesn't depend on the algorithm or data, but on the structure of the problem you are trying to learn. The lowest layers are always colors and spatial frequencies, which then combine into textures, and at a certain stage, geometric shapes emerge. The deeper.

question is, at what layer does this stop? If the universality hypothesis holds true, it means if you train a model with your own inputs and outputs, as long as you train it long enough, you will wake up inside that model. This is a quite shocking idea to Bach, but he doesn't know if it's true; perhaps language doesn't constrain the system generating it enough. But think about it , humans are inherently end-to-end trained learning systems. Biology has largely found a simple solution for generating your output based on your input. If you take a neural network and train it on the same input to produce a. similar output, it will eventually converge on a causal structure similar to yours. Of course, there are conditions where this might not hold true; for instance, some things run well on a brain but not on a GPU, and vice versa. Boch even says he believes GPUs are more powerful than brains, noting that with fast enough hardware, you can simulate any natural system to any degree, whereas the brain cannot simulate a digital computer. So, if our consciousness is a byproduct of the brain running complex intelligent processes, and computers don't need that same byproduct, computers might come up. with things smarter and more elegant than we do. In the conversation, there is also a topic regarding Bach's view on physicalism. He says physicalism consists of just two claims. First, reality has a causally closed mechanical layer that isn't driven by our consciousness; you can't just utter a spell and make the sun rise. Second, we are directly supervenient on this mechanical layer, not part of a simulation hypothesis where someone in a parent universe is running a server for us to live in like Minecraft. However, he adds a twist: matter isn't the bottom layer. No one has ever directly seen. matter or energy; they are just systemizations of observations, and our observations ultimately boil down to discernible differences, for which the technical term is information. Therefore , when talking about reality, information is fundamental. Physics is simply a layer of regularity we discovered within those information differences. He calls his position " cybernetic animism," meaning that animism doesn't necessarily have to be supernatural. The difference between a living system and a dead system is that the living system is occupied by a soul that has agency and can experience, and. this soul can be fully explained by information processing. So, physicalism and animism are not in conflict; he notes that almost all cultures other than our own are animistic cultures. The scientific worldview rejects the concept of spirits, yet clearly, some kind of spirit is at work within you and me. The question is not whether it exists, but how it works. As for how smart plants are or if they have sentience, he says he has no idea, noting it remains an open question. There are two other topics in this podcast that I find interesting; while not the main focus, they help us understand how Bach thinks.

. One is about the origin of the universe and error-correction models. His idea is that the universe exists because there is nothing to prevent it from existing. If there was nothing before the foundation of reality, then nothing could stop the universe from appearing. Therefore, the universe can neither be forced into existence by something preceding it, nor can it be prevented. Its existence is likely indeterminate, with both a branch where it exists and a branch where it does not . The branch that does not exist has no observers to complain; the branch that exists has observers. So, what can remain within the branch that exists? It. is the error-correcting pattern. He uses a bathtub as an analogy: you sit in the tub and wave your hand, causing various waves; most dissipate, but some circular vortices remain. It’s not that they are more probable, but that the information in the vortex loops back on itself, staying in a specific area of the water , thus gaining self-correction to persist until friction destroys it. At the base of the universe, these error-correcting patterns are particles ; they don't encounter friction, only colliding occasionally with others. One level up, particles interact to form molecules, and further up, cells. Cells. are super-molecules, but they possess something new: they can self-replicate to counter their own decay, rebuilding themselves to become more numerous. Bach believes that consciousness emerged as a colonizing pattern, not only replicating itself but making itself more real. It becomes "more real" by building machines that allow consciousness to persist, changing the surrounding reality and future by controlling how reality might thwart it. He mentions Stephen Wolfram and the computational limit of all possibilities; Bach suggests this pattern is exactly the superposition of. all automata that generate the universe . The ancient Greeks called it "Logos"— it is a math so simple that it needs no derivation and can exist on its own. Another topic is the philosophical zombie, a classic thought experiment. Is it possible for something to exist that behaves exactly like a human but has no subjective experience whatsoever? Bach says zombies are possible, and we already have them. Chess programs are one example; you cannot train a person to play chess without them being conscious. But you can train a computer to play. chess without it being conscious; computers can perform tasks that require human consciousness because the algorithms they run don't fit into the neural principles of your brain. However , zombies are not omnipotent. At some point, building a mindless entity to produce this behavior becomes even more complex than creating a conscious agent . He believes zombies are always possible, but sometimes it’s costlier to build a zombie, which is where his intuition differs from Searle's. Those two feel consciousness is incredibly complex because, to them, how.

consciousness functions isn't intuitive at all. Yet for him, this isn't counterintuitive, so he doesn't see what's so magical about consciousness— but how do you test that? Bark says if we build a system that behaves just like us, the question is whether we can produce the same behavior without phenomenology? If you scale a large model to be multimodal, it can produce similar outputs and observe itself, but if its reported self-observation differs from ours, we get counter-evidence. Moreover , if we build a system that reaches this. goal through self-organizing learning but find it can't achieve this organization self-organizingly—relying instead on imitation like current LLMs— that might prove consciousness is more complex. But this isn't definitive proof ; it could just mean he made a mistake. Even if a specific result isn't achieved , it doesn't mean it’s impossible, just that he failed to reach it. Therefore, negative proof is extremely hard to obtain; success, conversely, provides more supportive evidence. Because of this, he has already launched a large-scale initiative in California called the "California Institute for. Machine Consciousness." He is looking for people smarter than him willing to join a project to explore the search space of consciousness and see if we can build a self-organizing system capable of learning and developing phenomenology . Even if it turns out to be impossible , we’ll still learn something; this way , we can make progress by figuring out where we were wrong, rather than just where we were right. I spent nearly a week digesting this episode, and today I’m sharing what I believe is the most core part. Honestly, after hearing it, my biggest takeaway wasn't that AI is waking up, but that we still haven't. figured out what consciousness is actually doing. There’s a point Bark makes that I find very true: too few people truly dedicate their lives to studying consciousness. Most of our time is spent watching how many times the next model's parameters have doubled or whether the next benchmark can be passed , while few look back to ask the fundamental question: what is consciousness itself? Why does it exist ? And the latter, perhaps, is the key to determining what we can ultimately create. Thanks for watching, we'll.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 看見 AI 如何讓軟體開發門檻降低，並使「知道要解決什麼問題」比「會不會寫程式」更重要。
  • 透過 Supabase 的成長與產品轉型，了解 AI agents 正如何改變資料庫、開發工具與開源生態。
  • 從個人生活管理到巴西計程車司機打造叫車 App，認識非工程背景創作者如何把領域知識化為產品。
  • 思考未來每個人是否都需要自己的資料庫，以及個人資料自主權可能帶來的長遠影響。

摘要

AI agents 帶來成長轉折

作者介紹 Supabase 共同創辦人暨執行長 Paul Copplestone 與 YC 合夥人在 Latent Space 節目中的對談。Supabase 以開源 PostgreSQL 為基礎，已成為 CloudCode、Codex 等 AI agents 常用的資料庫平台。Paul 指出，Supabase 註冊用戶從一年前的 300 萬增至 1,300 萬，管理的資料庫也從 800 萬躍升至近 5,000 萬；每週新增超過 100 萬個資料庫，營收預計在今年成長四倍。更關鍵的是，約七成的新活動來自AI agents，顯示市場正跨過新的轉折點。

從控制台優先，走向程式碼優先

Paul 將 Supabase 的產品發展分成幾個階段：最初受到 Airtable 啟發，採取控制台優先的設計；到了約 2021 年，因客戶需要大量建立資料庫，團隊轉向API 優先，而這項選擇後來也支援了 Bolt.new 等產品。如今，使用者不再常進入控制台，agents 也需要在程式碼與終端機環境中操作，因此 Supabase 正進一步轉型為程式碼優先、以 Git 為核心的平台。控制台中的功能也應能透過程式碼同步，實踐基礎設施即程式碼的概念。

開源讓工具更容易被採用

Supabase 得以成長，也受惠於產業前浪鋪路：Parse 與 Firebase 讓市場看見獨立後端平台的可能，Heroku 推廣了 Postgres，MongoDB 則帶動 NoSQL 的普及。Paul 認為，開源是 Supabase 擴大影響力的重要原因；團隊支持 Prisma 等 Postgres 生態系工具，接觸到更廣泛的開發社群。對 agents 而言，開源尤其實用：遇到問題時，它們能直接查看原始碼，而不是被封閉系統擋在外面。企業也能藉由檢視原始碼確認安全性。

創作者與領域專家加入開發行列

Supabase 不只吸引工程師，也迎來愈來愈多沒有傳統軟體背景的創作者。Paul 觀察到，今年註冊人數快速增加的同時，啟用與轉換等指標也同步向上，原因是模型能力進步，讓更多人能親手打造產品。YC 合夥人 Harj Taggar 分享，自己過去雖能寫簡單腳本，複雜軟體仍得依賴工程師；如今卻能自行開發個人財務管理工具，並從頭串接銀行 API。Paul 認為，這些領域專家特別適合成為創作者，因為他們最清楚自己所在領域尚未解決的問題。Supabase Select 會上，一名約 50 歲的巴西計程車司機甚至只用手機，就打造出服務當地市場的叫車 App。

從「需要技術共同創辦人」到「知道要做什麼」

Garry Tan 回顧 YC 的觀念轉變：過去幾年，YC 特別強調新創需要技術共同創辦人；近來則愈來愈重視創作者本身。當開發能力變得隨時可取得，真正稀缺的就不再只是工程能力，而是判斷該打造什麼。許多需求過去明明存在、也可能有客戶，卻因為找不到工程師而沒有被實現。如今更多人可以直接動手，而這些新產品與創作者最終也都需要資料庫。

個人資料庫成為生活中樞

Harj 分享自己打造名為「Control Tower」的個人系統，涵蓋生活中的多種資料與工作流程，包括整理電子郵件、追蹤支出與管理健康紀錄。他起初希望把資料都放在 Markdown 檔案裡，但後來發現資料庫已不可或缺。這套只為一人打造的金融模組，能運用個人脈絡辨識交易對象並正確分類，某些方面甚至勝過一般理財產品。使用者也能透過電子郵件或上傳介面交付檔案，再由 agent 判斷檔案內容與處理方式，最後集中存放在 Supabase。Harj 認為，金融與健康是人們最希望掌握自身資料的領域；資料庫的價值，在於成為可靠的個人資料來源，讓使用者能在其上建置不同應用與 agents。

從原型走向大規模資料庫服務

Paul 以 GPT 每週約 12 億名使用者推想：若每個人每月都想推出一個產品，資料庫需求便可能達到每月 12 億個，遠高於 Supabase 現在每週約 100 萬個的建立量。面對這種規模，他認為 PostgreSQL 仍有發展空間，但架構必須調整。團隊收購 Deno 後，將利用其能與 Postgres、SQLite 相容的架構，推出面向新創工作負載的 Supabase Spark。核心承諾仍是讓使用者從同一套體驗起步，並隨需求一路擴展，呼應「從原型到 PB 級規模」的願景。對談最後也提到，資料庫公司過去常以成為 Oracle、迅速進入企業市場為目標；但 AI 時代如何同時服務各種規模的使用者，仍是重要課題。

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. Imagine, what would the world look like if everyone could turn the ideas in their heads into software? Supabase co-founder and CEO Paul Copplestone recently spent 49 minutes on the Latent Space podcast. Supabase is a backend platform based on open-source PostgreSQL, and today it has become the default database for agents like CloudCode and Codex. The hosts of this conversation were Garry Tan, Harj Taggar , and Jared Friedman, all of whom are core partners at Y Combinator. They. weren't talking about just an ordinary database company, but about how the entire industry is changing now that AI is lowering the barrier for software developers to zero. Let me share some numbers: Supabase now has 13 million registered users, a figure that was only 3 million just 12 months ago. It manages nearly 50 million databases, up from 8 million during the same period last year . Over 1 million databases are created every week, and this year's revenue is set to quadruple. Most notably, about 70 %of new activity comes from AI agents; Paul describes this as a tipping point. So, how did this tipping point come about? Garry offered an observation: startups joining YC on their first day receive a T-shirt that says "Make something people want." But now, it should be changed to "Make something agents want." Supabase is a perfect example of this. Paul's assessment is that growth comes from two main directions: first, software engineers are developing with fewer constraints, and second, more and more non-engineer creators are getting involved. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 看見 AI 如何讓軟體開發門檻降低，並使「知道要解決什麼問題」比「會不會寫程式」更重要。
  • 透過 Supabase 的成長與產品轉型，了解 AI agents 正如何改變資料庫、開發工具與開源生態。
  • 從個人生活管理到巴西計程車司機打造叫車 App，認識非工程背景創作者如何把領域知識化為產品。
  • 思考未來每個人是否都需要自己的資料庫，以及個人資料自主權可能帶來的長遠影響。

摘要

AI agents 帶來成長轉折

作者介紹 Supabase 共同創辦人暨執行長 Paul Copplestone 與 YC 合夥人在 Latent Space 節目中的對談。Supabase 以開源 PostgreSQL 為基礎，已成為 CloudCode、Codex 等 AI agents 常用的資料庫平台。Paul 指出，Supabase 註冊用戶從一年前的 300 萬增至 1,300 萬，管理的資料庫也從 800 萬躍升至近 5,000 萬；每週新增超過 100 萬個資料庫，營收預計在今年成長四倍。更關鍵的是，約七成的新活動來自AI agents，顯示市場正跨過新的轉折點。

從控制台優先，走向程式碼優先

Paul 將 Supabase 的產品發展分成幾個階段：最初受到 Airtable 啟發，採取控制台優先的設計；到了約 2021 年，因客戶需要大量建立資料庫，團隊轉向API 優先，而這項選擇後來也支援了 Bolt.new 等產品。如今，使用者不再常進入控制台，agents 也需要在程式碼與終端機環境中操作，因此 Supabase 正進一步轉型為程式碼優先、以 Git 為核心的平台。控制台中的功能也應能透過程式碼同步，實踐基礎設施即程式碼的概念。

開源讓工具更容易被採用

Supabase 得以成長，也受惠於產業前浪鋪路：Parse 與 Firebase 讓市場看見獨立後端平台的可能，Heroku 推廣了 Postgres，MongoDB 則帶動 NoSQL 的普及。Paul 認為，開源是 Supabase 擴大影響力的重要原因；團隊支持 Prisma 等 Postgres 生態系工具，接觸到更廣泛的開發社群。對 agents 而言，開源尤其實用：遇到問題時，它們能直接查看原始碼，而不是被封閉系統擋在外面。企業也能藉由檢視原始碼確認安全性。

創作者與領域專家加入開發行列

Supabase 不只吸引工程師，也迎來愈來愈多沒有傳統軟體背景的創作者。Paul 觀察到，今年註冊人數快速增加的同時，啟用與轉換等指標也同步向上，原因是模型能力進步，讓更多人能親手打造產品。YC 合夥人 Harj Taggar 分享，自己過去雖能寫簡單腳本，複雜軟體仍得依賴工程師；如今卻能自行開發個人財務管理工具，並從頭串接銀行 API。Paul 認為，這些領域專家特別適合成為創作者，因為他們最清楚自己所在領域尚未解決的問題。Supabase Select 會上，一名約 50 歲的巴西計程車司機甚至只用手機，就打造出服務當地市場的叫車 App。

從「需要技術共同創辦人」到「知道要做什麼」

Garry Tan 回顧 YC 的觀念轉變：過去幾年，YC 特別強調新創需要技術共同創辦人；近來則愈來愈重視創作者本身。當開發能力變得隨時可取得，真正稀缺的就不再只是工程能力，而是判斷該打造什麼。許多需求過去明明存在、也可能有客戶，卻因為找不到工程師而沒有被實現。如今更多人可以直接動手，而這些新產品與創作者最終也都需要資料庫。

個人資料庫成為生活中樞

Harj 分享自己打造名為「Control Tower」的個人系統，涵蓋生活中的多種資料與工作流程，包括整理電子郵件、追蹤支出與管理健康紀錄。他起初希望把資料都放在 Markdown 檔案裡，但後來發現資料庫已不可或缺。這套只為一人打造的金融模組，能運用個人脈絡辨識交易對象並正確分類，某些方面甚至勝過一般理財產品。使用者也能透過電子郵件或上傳介面交付檔案，再由 agent 判斷檔案內容與處理方式，最後集中存放在 Supabase。Harj 認為，金融與健康是人們最希望掌握自身資料的領域；資料庫的價值，在於成為可靠的個人資料來源，讓使用者能在其上建置不同應用與 agents。

從原型走向大規模資料庫服務

Paul 以 GPT 每週約 12 億名使用者推想：若每個人每月都想推出一個產品，資料庫需求便可能達到每月 12 億個，遠高於 Supabase 現在每週約 100 萬個的建立量。面對這種規模，他認為 PostgreSQL 仍有發展空間，但架構必須調整。團隊收購 Deno 後，將利用其能與 Postgres、SQLite 相容的架構，推出面向新創工作負載的 Supabase Spark。核心承諾仍是讓使用者從同一套體驗起步，並隨需求一路擴展，呼應「從原型到 PB 級規模」的願景。對談最後也提到，資料庫公司過去常以成為 Oracle、迅速進入企業市場為目標；但 AI 時代如何同時服務各種規模的使用者，仍是重要課題。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 看見 AI 如何讓軟體開發門檻降低，並使「知道要解決什麼問題」比「會不會寫程式」更重要。
  • 透過 Supabase 的成長與產品轉型，了解 AI agents 正如何改變資料庫、開發工具與開源生態。
  • 從個人生活管理到巴西計程車司機打造叫車 App，認識非工程背景創作者如何把領域知識化為產品。
  • 思考未來每個人是否都需要自己的資料庫，以及個人資料自主權可能帶來的長遠影響。

摘要

AI agents 帶來成長轉折

作者介紹 Supabase 共同創辦人暨執行長 Paul Copplestone 與 YC 合夥人在 Latent Space 節目中的對談。Supabase 以開源 PostgreSQL 為基礎，已成為 CloudCode、Codex 等 AI agents 常用的資料庫平台。Paul 指出，Supabase 註冊用戶從一年前的 300 萬增至 1,300 萬，管理的資料庫也從 800 萬躍升至近 5,000 萬；每週新增超過 100 萬個資料庫，營收預計在今年成長四倍。更關鍵的是，約七成的新活動來自AI agents，顯示市場正跨過新的轉折點。

從控制台優先，走向程式碼優先

Paul 將 Supabase 的產品發展分成幾個階段：最初受到 Airtable 啟發，採取控制台優先的設計；到了約 2021 年，因客戶需要大量建立資料庫，團隊轉向API 優先，而這項選擇後來也支援了 Bolt.new 等產品。如今，使用者不再常進入控制台，agents 也需要在程式碼與終端機環境中操作，因此 Supabase 正進一步轉型為程式碼優先、以 Git 為核心的平台。控制台中的功能也應能透過程式碼同步，實踐基礎設施即程式碼的概念。

開源讓工具更容易被採用

Supabase 得以成長，也受惠於產業前浪鋪路：Parse 與 Firebase 讓市場看見獨立後端平台的可能，Heroku 推廣了 Postgres，MongoDB 則帶動 NoSQL 的普及。Paul 認為，開源是 Supabase 擴大影響力的重要原因；團隊支持 Prisma 等 Postgres 生態系工具，接觸到更廣泛的開發社群。對 agents 而言，開源尤其實用：遇到問題時，它們能直接查看原始碼，而不是被封閉系統擋在外面。企業也能藉由檢視原始碼確認安全性。

創作者與領域專家加入開發行列

Supabase 不只吸引工程師，也迎來愈來愈多沒有傳統軟體背景的創作者。Paul 觀察到，今年註冊人數快速增加的同時，啟用與轉換等指標也同步向上，原因是模型能力進步，讓更多人能親手打造產品。YC 合夥人 Harj Taggar 分享，自己過去雖能寫簡單腳本，複雜軟體仍得依賴工程師；如今卻能自行開發個人財務管理工具，並從頭串接銀行 API。Paul 認為，這些領域專家特別適合成為創作者，因為他們最清楚自己所在領域尚未解決的問題。Supabase Select 會上，一名約 50 歲的巴西計程車司機甚至只用手機，就打造出服務當地市場的叫車 App。

從「需要技術共同創辦人」到「知道要做什麼」

Garry Tan 回顧 YC 的觀念轉變：過去幾年，YC 特別強調新創需要技術共同創辦人；近來則愈來愈重視創作者本身。當開發能力變得隨時可取得，真正稀缺的就不再只是工程能力，而是判斷該打造什麼。許多需求過去明明存在、也可能有客戶，卻因為找不到工程師而沒有被實現。如今更多人可以直接動手，而這些新產品與創作者最終也都需要資料庫。

個人資料庫成為生活中樞

Harj 分享自己打造名為「Control Tower」的個人系統，涵蓋生活中的多種資料與工作流程，包括整理電子郵件、追蹤支出與管理健康紀錄。他起初希望把資料都放在 Markdown 檔案裡，但後來發現資料庫已不可或缺。這套只為一人打造的金融模組，能運用個人脈絡辨識交易對象並正確分類，某些方面甚至勝過一般理財產品。使用者也能透過電子郵件或上傳介面交付檔案，再由 agent 判斷檔案內容與處理方式，最後集中存放在 Supabase。Harj 認為，金融與健康是人們最希望掌握自身資料的領域；資料庫的價值，在於成為可靠的個人資料來源，讓使用者能在其上建置不同應用與 agents。

從原型走向大規模資料庫服務

Paul 以 GPT 每週約 12 億名使用者推想：若每個人每月都想推出一個產品，資料庫需求便可能達到每月 12 億個，遠高於 Supabase 現在每週約 100 萬個的建立量。面對這種規模，他認為 PostgreSQL 仍有發展空間，但架構必須調整。團隊收購 Deno 後，將利用其能與 Postgres、SQLite 相容的架構，推出面向新創工作負載的 Supabase Spark。核心承諾仍是讓使用者從同一套體驗起步，並隨需求一路擴展，呼應「從原型到 PB 級規模」的願景。對談最後也提到，資料庫公司過去常以成為 Oracle、迅速進入企業市場為目標；但 AI 時代如何同時服務各種規模的使用者，仍是重要課題。
